articles.title: Comparative Effects of Pharmacological Treatment on Heart Failure with Mildly Reduced or Preserved Ejection Fraction: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The comparative efficacy and safety of the new drugs (including sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors [SGLT-2Is], glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists [GLP-1RAs], non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists [nsMRAs], and soluble guanylate cyclase stimulators [sGCs]) for heart failure with mildly reduced or preserved (HFmrEF/HFpEF) ejection fraction remains largely unclear. We conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis to evaluate their comparative effects on HFmrEF/HFpEF, aiming to provide evidence-based guidance for treatment selection. METHODS: MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were comprehensively searched. We included randomized controlled trials that compared nsMRA, sGC, SGLT-2I, and GLP-1RA with placebo for patients with HFmrEF/HFpEF. Primary efficacy outcomes were cardiovascular (CV) death, hospitalization for heart failure (HF hospitalization), and all-cause mortality, while primary safety outcomes were adverse events (AEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs). The main analysis was conducted to compare the effects on HFmrEF/HFpEF between individual drugs. A frequentist network meta-analysis with random-effects models was used to calculate risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous outcomes and standardized mean differences (SMDs) for continuous outcomes. RESULTS: A total of 20 randomized controlled trials (RCTs, including 10 drugs from 35 publications) were included for analyses, but none provided head-to-head direct comparisons. No significant differences among all the individual drugs were found in risks of CV death or all-cause mortality. Compared with exenatide, low or moderate certainty evidence showed that dapagliflozin (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.36-0.91), empagliflozin (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.34-0.86), and semaglutide (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.20-0.91) were related to decreased risk of HF hospitalization. No significant differences in the risk of SAEs were found among the individual drugs. Compared with empagliflozin, very low certainty evidence showed that tirzepatide (RR 1.17, 95% CI 1.04-1.32) was related to increased risk of AEs. When comparing the four drug classes (nsMRA, sGC, SGLT-2I, and GLP-1RA), no significant differences in efficacy outcomes were found, while SGLT-2I (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78-0.96) was associated with a decreased risk of AEs compared with GLP-1RA. CONCLUSIONS: No significant differences among the individual SGLT-2I, GLP-1RA, nsMRA, and sGC drugs were found in risks of CV death, all-cause mortality or SAEs in patients with HFmrEF/HFpEF. Further evidence is needed to support these comparative effects and update guidance on medication choice for HFmrEF/HFpEF. REGISTRATION: PROSPERO identifier number CRD420251143542.

articles.title: Patients with Chronic Inflammatory Diseases Can Experience Higher Exposure of Small Molecule Drugs than Healthy Volunteers: An Analysis of Recently Approved Drugs.
articles.abstract: Chronic inflammation has long been known to downregulate the activity of certain cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes-the main enzymes responsible for the phase I metabolism of many small molecule drugs-potentially leading to higher exposures in patients with chronic inflammatory diseases compared to healthy volunteers. Neglecting this potential difference in the pharmacokinetics can have several implications for dose translation from healthy volunteers to proof of concept studies in patients: sub-optimal design of dose-ranging studies and increased risk of adverse events due to overprediction of safety margins. Yet this disease-drug interaction has rarely been prospectively considered in drug development in the past. This review aims to quantify the extent of decreased (apparent) clearance in patients compared to healthy volunteers of small molecule drugs that were approved by the FDA in the past 15 years for important chronic inflammatory indications. Based on reported population pharmacokinetic analyses, 25% (5 of 20) of small molecule drugs approved for the selected indications showed a meaningfully higher area under the curve (AUC) by more than 25% in patients compared to healthy volunteers. As a common feature, all five drugs are primarily metabolized by CYP3A4 or CYP2C19 and for four of the five drugs, the contribution of metabolism to their elimination is more than 50%. These findings highlight the need to assess a drug's susceptibility to changes in the metabolic activity under chronic inflammation when translating dose predictions from healthy volunteers to patients.

articles.title: Scutellarin as a multi-target neuroprotective agent: analytical evidence, pharmacokinetic insights and translational strategies across neurodegenerative disorders.
articles.abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders are a leading cause of disability and mortality globally, but effective disease-modifying therapeutic strategies are still largely unavailable. Scutellarin is a flavonoid glycoside extracted from Erigeron breviscapus (Vant.) Hand-Mazz. It has been widely studied in preclinical models of neurodegenerative disorders. In this study, we performed a systematic review of preclinical animal studies. We combined comprehensive database retrieval with quantitative synthesis of eligible outcomes. The pooled results demonstrated that scutellarin significantly reduced cerebral infarct volume and improved neurological deficit scores in cerebral ischemia-reperfusion models. It also ameliorated learning and memory impairments in experimental Alzheimer's disease (AD) models. Consistent neuroprotective effects were also found in models of depression, anxiety, Parkinson's disease, etc. Mechanistic analysis indicated that scutellarin produces multi-level neuroprotective effects. It acts by reducing oxidative stress, inhibiting neuroinflammation, suppressing apoptosis, stabilizing the neurovascular unit and other neurobiological processes. This review first evaluated the preclinical efficacy of scutellarin through systematic review and meta-analysis. It then integrated cross-disease mechanisms with network pharmacology, reverse virtual screening and molecular docking to identify computationally predicted targets. Although scutellarin shows promising preclinical effects, its clinical translation faces major limitations. These limitations include low oral bioavailability, poor blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration and insufficient data on brain exposure. Overall, scutellarin is a multi-target neuroprotective candidate. Future studies should focus on target validation, exposure-response modeling, delivery optimization and clinically relevant translational evaluation.

articles.title: Effects of Probiotic Supplementation on Depression, Anxiety, and Sleep Quality in Healthy Participants: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the effects of probiotic supplementation on depression, anxiety, and sleep quality in healthy adults. PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Embase were searched from inception to September 18, 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing probiotics with placebo for ≥4 weeks were included. Data from 20 studies involving 1,508 participants were analyzed using Stata 17.0. Random-effects or fixed-effects models were selected according to heterogeneity. The GRADE approach was used to assess evidence certainty. Probiotics significantly reduced depression scores (SMD = -0.23, 95% CI: -0.36 to -0.10, P < 0.01; I² = 4.67%) and improved sleep quality (SMD = -0.37, 95% CI: -0.52 to -0.22, P < 0.01; I² = 41.67%). However, the overall effect on anxiety was not significant (SMD = -0.11, 95% CI: -0.31 to 0.09, P = 0.27; I² = 61.41%). Subgroup analyses were exploratory and unadjusted; no definitive conclusion can be drawn regarding intervention duration or strain type. GRADE certainty was moderate for depression and sleep quality, but very low for anxiety. In conclusion, probiotic supplementation may alleviate depressive symptoms and improve sleep quality in healthy adults, whereas its effect on anxiety remains inconclusive. Larger, standardized RCTs are needed to confirm these findings and clarify strain-specific effects.

articles.title: Unfolded Protein Response Pathway in Neurodegenerative Diseases: Genetic Insights into the Mechanisms Linking UPR Dysregulation to Tau Pathology and Therapeutic Implications.
articles.abstract: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress activates a dynamic signaling network known as the unfolded protein response (UPR), which aims to reestablish cellular protein homeostasis and promote cell survival during stress. Dysregulated UPR signaling has been increasingly implicated in neurodegenerative diseases, many of which are characterized by tau hyperphosphorylation, misfolding, aggregation, and impaired clearance, contributing to neuronal dysfunction and degeneration. Genetic variations in UPR pathway components and their downstream effectors may influence the magnitude, duration, and cellular consequences of ER stress responses, thereby shaping disease susceptibility, progression, and therapeutic response. This review examines genetic variation within the UPR pathway and its relevance to the pathophysiology of tau-associated neurodegenerative diseases. By integrating evidence from genetic, cellular, and disease-model studies, we highlight how UPR dysregulation represents an important mechanistic interface linking genetic susceptibility with cellular stress responses, proteostasis disruption, and tau pathology. The article further explores UPR-focused therapeutic approaches, emphasizing how understanding genetic variation may provide insights into disease mechanisms and identify potential therapeutic targets. Building on these findings, we propose a framework in which UPR dysregulation is viewed not merely as a passive cellular response to neurodegeneration, but as a potential mechanistic determinant linking genetic risk to altered stress adaptation, proteostatic imbalance, and tau pathology. Within this framework, genetic variation in UPR components may contribute to distinct disease-relevant UPR states and influence therapeutic responsiveness. Integrating genetic variation with functional UPR signatures and treatment response may ultimately reveal disease-relevant therapeutic opportunities and inform the development of more precise UPR-targeted strategies for tau-associated neurodegenerative diseases.

articles.title: Evaluating the Association Between PPI Use and Dementia Risk Considering Methodological Choices: An Updated Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), commonly prescribed for gastrointestinal disorders, have been investigated for their association with the risk of dementia. We aimed to assess the association between PPI use and dementia risk in older adults and examine the influence of methodological choices on this association. We conducted a meta-analysis of longitudinal observational studies, including subgroup analyses to address time-related biases and comparator selection. Relevant studies were systematically searched in the MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL databases from their inception to January 25, 2026. Twenty-three studies of older adults without dementia at baseline, reporting adjusted estimates for PPI users versus a comparator group, met the inclusion criteria. The pooled hazard ratio (HR) indicated a modest association between PPI use and dementia (HR = 1.18, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.02-1.37). Dementia risk did not differ significantly between PPI users and users of histamine-2 receptor antagonists (H2RAs) (HR = 1.04, 95% CI 0.89-1.20). In a post hoc analysis, H2RA use itself was associated with dementia (HR = 1.44, 95% CI 1.07-1.93), whereas excluding H2RA-treated patients strengthened the PPI estimate (HR = 1.75, 95% CI 1.38-2.22). Estimates also differed according to how time-related bias was handled: lag time, HR = 1.25, 95% CI 1.07-1.46; time-varying exposure, HR = 1.38, 95% CI 1.16-1.64. PPI use was modestly associated with incident dementia. However, the strength and specificity depended substantially on comparator selection and handling of time-related bias. Well-designed, long-term studies using active comparators are needed to clarify whether this effect is PPI-specific.

Twelve-Month Cumulative Incidence, Characteristics, and Correlates of Non-adherence in Youths Treated with Second-Generation Antipsychotics for Mental Disorders: Results from a Prospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Antipsychotic non-adherence in youths with mental disorders is multifactorial, may remain clinically unnoticed, and has been underresearched. OBJECTIVE: To characterize antipsychotic non-adherence in youths, including its correlates. METHOD: Data were collected from the naturalistic Second-Generation Antipsychotic Treatment Indications, Effectiveness and Tolerability in Youth (SATIETY) cohort study, which included youths (ages 4-17 years) who initiated clinician's choice second-generation antipsychotics (SGAs) for psychosis-, mood-, or disruptive behavior-spectrum disorders and had ≥ 1 outpatient day of follow-up. Non-adherence was assessed via interview and antipsychotic plasma levels, and cumulative rates were analyzed via Kaplan-Meyer survival analysis and observed incidences. Characteristics of non-adherence and non-adherent patients were examined. Three multivariable regression models were used to identify predictors of observed cumulative non-adherence over 12 months. RESULTS: Altogether, 521 youths (median age 14.9 years; male 55.1%; post-pubertal 72.7%; antipsychotic-naïve 65.5%; inpatients 74.7%; mood-spectrum disorder 56.5%, schizophrenia-spectrum disorder 22.9%, aggression-spectrum disorder 20.6%) started risperidone (37.2%), aripiprazole (26.9%), quetiapine (22.8%), or olanzapine (13.1%). The observed 12-month cumulative SGA non-adherence (occurring after a median follow-up of 75 days, interquartile range [IQR] 30-135 days) was 24.4% (overt 61.4%, covert/blood level-detected 38.6%; decision by: patient 75.6%, caregiver 18.1%, both 6.3%), increasing to 36.2% (95% confidence interval [CI] 30.4-41.9%) in the survival analysis. Non-mutually exclusive reasons for non-adherence, defined as SGA discontinuation against medical advice, included perceived lack of SGA treatment need (87.4%), intolerability (22.1%), and/or inefficacy (4.7%). In the first multivariable model in the full dataset, non-adherence was predicted by substance use disorder (odds ratio [OR] 3.38; 95% CI 1.85-6.17), non-white origin (OR 1.62; 95% CI 1.04-2.52), more last visit psychotropic medications (OR 1.60; 95% CI 1.27-2.00), and shorter pre-baseline lifetime antipsychotic treatment (OR 1.09; 95% CI 1.00-1.13 per month) (n = 515, r2 = 0.10, p < 0.0001). Including non-dual-biological parent household (available in n = 435) in the second, exploratory model, non-dual-biological parent household and the four predictors of the first model predicted non-adherence (r2 = 0.13, p < 0.0001). Finally, including last visit patient and caregiver Drug Attitude Inventory (DAI)-30/DAI-10 ratings (available in n = 273) to the third, exploratory model, substance use disorder, non-dual-biological parent household, more last visit psychiatric medications, worse last visit DAI-30 patient ratings, and risperidone treatment predicted non-adherence (r2 = 0.17, p < 0.0001). CONCLUSIONS: One in four youths starting SGAs (increasing in survival analyses accounting for early dropouts to more than one in three youth) discontinued SGAs against medical advice within 12 months, mainly owing to perceived lack of treatment need. As much as 39% of the non-adherence would have remained undetected without SGA plasma level assessments. Interventions should target patient, caregiver, and medication factors to reduce barriers and improve outcomes.

articles.title: Efficacy of Epimedii Folium and related preparations in experimental osteoporosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Epimedii Folium and related extracts have shown osteogenic, antiresorptive, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory activities in experimental studies. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated their efficacy in rodent models of osteoporosis. METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, and Wanfang Data were searched from their inception to 13 June 2026. Controlled in vivo studies using rat or mouse models of osteoporosis or experimentally induced bone loss were eligible. Random-effects models generated Hedges' standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The risk of bias was assessed using the SYRCLE tool. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261428223). Sensitivity analyses examined heterogeneity, the influence of the Qi 2019 estimate, and the effects of multi-arm dependence, preparation type, disease model, duration, and dose. Certainty was appraised using an adaptation of GRADE for preclinical animal evidence. RESULTS: Twenty-nine independent rodent studies were included. Femoral BMD increased (20 comparisons from 9 studies; SMD = 1.66, 95% CI: 1.07-2.25; 95% prediction interval [PI]: -0.61 to 3.93; I2 = 73.77%). Excluding Qi 2019 reduced the SMD to 1.44 (95% CI: 0.96-1.92), while a three-level study-cluster robust model yielded an SMD of 2.25 (95% CI: 0.40-4.10). The average effects favored several regional BMD, microarchitectural, and biomechanical outcomes, but the majority of PIs crossed the null. PINP was not significant. The Systematic Review Centre for Laboratory Animal Experimentation (SYRCLE) assessment found that the majority of judgments were unclear, with nine domain-level judgments rated as high risk; certainty was very low. CONCLUSION: Random-effects pooled estimates favored the examined oral Epimedii Folium-derived preparations for several regional BMD, trabecular microarchitecture, and ex vivo biomechanical outcomes in rodent models. However, wide prediction intervals, chemical and model heterogeneity, small study sizes, incomplete reporting, and correlated multi-arm comparisons limit confidence in the pooled effect magnitudes. Chemically standardized preparations and exposure-informed dosing are needed before clinical translation. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261428223, identifier CRD420261428223.

articles.title: Associations of glucose- and lipid-lowering medications with incident or first-recorded psoriasis: a systematic review of real-world observational studies.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Glucose-lowering and lipid-lowering medications may influence psoriasis development through metabolic, inflammatory, and immune pathways, but real-world evidence remains inconsistent. OBJECTIVE: To systematically evaluate associations between these medications and the risk of incident or first-recorded psoriasis, with particular attention to comparator choice, outcome definition, study design, and data-source overlap. METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to 1 July 2026, with an updated search conducted on 11 September 2026 during manuscript revision. Longitudinal observational studies evaluating glucose-lowering or lipid-lowering medication use and incident or first-recorded psoriasis were included. Evidence was grouped by medication class, comparator, and outcome type and synthesized narratively. Psoriasis-specific outcomes and broader or composite psoriatic-disease outcomes were treated as distinct evidence categories. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I. Meta-analysis was not performed because sufficiently comparable and mutually independent estimates were unavailable within most medication-comparator-outcome strata. RESULTS: Eighteen reports were included. Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor estimates were generally below 1; in an active-comparator study using a broader psoriasis-related outcome including psoriatic arthritis codes, the hazard ratio versus sulfonylureas was 0.422 (95% confidence interval, 0.273-0.716). Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist estimates were notably comparator dependent: estimates were above 1 in comparisons with dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors, approximately null in comparison with sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors, and inconsistent across comparisons with GLP-1RA nonuse. Most sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor estimates were near or above the null. Metformin and thiazolidinediones yielded lower estimates in some studies, whereas statins showed no consistent association or exposure-response gradient. Of the 18 report-level ROBINS-I assessment anchors, 13 (72.2%) had a serious overall risk of bias and five (27.8%) had a moderate risk; none had a low risk of bias. Several reports may also have included overlapping populations and were therefore not interpreted as independent replications. CONCLUSION: The available observational evidence does not establish causal effects of glucose-lowering or lipid-lowering medications on incident or first-recorded psoriasis. This review does not support choosing or avoiding these medications solely to prevent psoriasis or modifying standard diabetes or cardiovascular treatment on the basis of the reported associations. The findings remain hypothesis-generating because of confounding by indication, other risks of bias, and limited independent evidence. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://doi.org/10.37766/inplasy2026.7.0070, identifier INPLASY202670070.

articles.title: Risk prediction models for prolonged postoperative opioid use: a systematic review and meta-analysis of drug-risk stratification, validation and evidence benchmarks.
articles.abstract: UNLABELLED: Prolonged postoperative opioid use represents a medication-safety problem in which short-term μ-opioid receptor agonist exposure may transition to sustained consumption, tolerance, opioid-induced hyperalgesia and dependence in susceptible patients. Risk prediction models could support clinical pharmacology-informed opioid stewardship by identifying patients who require individualised dosing, closer follow-up, alternative analgesic strategies or deprescribing support. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus and the Cochrane Library from inception to 5 July 2026 for studies developing or validating multivariable models predicting opioid use beyond 30 days after surgery. One primary estimate was selected per independent cohort. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) values were logit-transformed and pooled using random-effects restricted maximum likelihood models with Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals. 35 reports met the eligibility criteria and contributed 35 independent AUROC estimates to the quantitative synthesis. The pooled AUROC was 0.794 (95% CI 0.751-0.832), although between-study heterogeneity was extreme (I2 = 99%; 95% prediction interval, 0.512-0.934). Exploratory analyses suggested numerically lower discrimination in externally or temporally validated models and in opioid-naive cohorts, but these findings were not consistently supported by meta-regression. Current models identify a measurable drug-risk signal, yet few meet all four predefined translational-evidence benchmarks, and insufficient validation, calibration and clinical-utility evidence limits their immediate use for individualised opioid pharmacotherapy. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261442043, identifier CRD420261442043.

articles.title: Phytochemistry, pharmacology, safety, and applications of Buddleja globosa Hope [Scrophulariaceae]: a systematic review from bioactive metabolites and mechanisms to translational perspectives.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Buddleja globosa Hope [Scrophulariaceae] is a shrub native to South America, known in Chile as matico or pañil. Its leaves are widely used in traditional medicine and have commercial applications, primarily as aqueous extracts administered orally or topically. Its use is supported by over a century of traditional practice, and it is one of the few native species recognized as a traditional herbal medicine in Chile based on long-standing use and emerging scientific evidence. METHODOLOGY: We retrieved bibliographic data on the traditional uses, ethnopharmacology, phytochemistry, and biological activities of B. globosa from Web of Science®, Scopus®, PubMed®, SciFinder®, University of Chile Repository® and grey literature. We conducted a systematic review in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION: Fifty studies were included in the systematic review. Traditional uses have made B. globosa one of the most important medicinal plant species in Chile for both internal and topical applications, although the strength of evidence varies by indication. Its use in treating gastric ulcers and promoting skin wound healing is particularly noteworthy, with pharmacological activities reported in in vitro studies, murine models, and clinical trials. The species contains a remarkable diversity of bioactive metabolites (n = 119), including verbascoside, echinacoside, buddledin A, α-amyrin, β-amyrin, luteolin, and apigenin; however, its essential oil remains poorly characterized. Furthermore, the review identified important knowledge gaps, particularly in medicinal cultivation and silvicultural management, chemical standardization, metabolomic variability, toxicological and safety assessment, and preclinical and clinical validation. Addressing these gaps will be essential to support the development of standardized phytotherapeutic products based on B. globosa. CONCLUSION: Buddleja globosa represents a strategic medicinal resource due to its long history of traditional use, its widespread use in Chile, and the growing body of scientific evidence suggesting its biological properties, particularly in wound-healing applications. This review documents several bioactive metabolites, including verbascoside, amyrins, and flavonoids. In this context, future research should focus on strategies that promote knowledge transfer and on developing public policies to implement Good Manufacturing Practices, translating their use into evidence-based healthcare. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261450024.

articles.title: Efficacy and safety of Yangxin Dingji capsule as an adjunctive therapy for atrial fibrillation: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Yangxin Dingji Capsule (YXDJ), a modern Chinese patent medicine derived from the classic Zhigancao Decoction, is commonly used as an adjuvant therapy for atrial fibrillation (AF). This study aimed to comprehensively evaluate the efficacy and safety of YXDJ as an adjuvant therapy in AF patients. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, China Biology Medicine, Wanfang, VIP Chinese Journal Service Platform, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure from inception to 1 April 2026, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing YXDJ plus conventional therapy versus conventional therapy alone in patients with AF. Meta-analyses were performed using RevMan with fixed- or random-effects models based on heterogeneity. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool, and the overall quality of evidence for each outcome was evaluated using the GRADE framework. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261286691). RESULTS: Ten RCTs involving 872 patients were included. All studies were Chinese-language publications with methodological limitations. According to the RoB 2 assessment, most studies were rated as having some concerns or high risk of bias, mainly due to inadequate allocation concealment, lack of blinding for subjective outcomes, and absence of publicly available trial registrations or protocols. In terms of clinical symptoms, YXDJ was associated with improvements in the overall clinical response rate [RR = 1.27, P < 0.00001, very low], reductions in EHRA symptom scores [MD = -0.47, P = 0.0009, very low], and reductions in postoperative AF recurrence at 6 months [RR = 0.43, P = 0.03, moderate]. For cardiac function, YXDJ was associated with increases in left atrial ejection fraction (LAEF) [MD = 2.11%, P = 0.003, low] and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) [MD = 4.39%, P < 0.00001, moderate], whereas no significant changes were observed in left atrial diameter (LAD) [MD = -1.97 mm, P = 0.07, very low] and mitral E/A ratio [MD = 0.12, P = 0.06, very low]; subgroup analysis revealed that YXDJ reduced LAD in postoperative patients [MD = -2.70 mm, P = 0.02, low]. In terms of inflammatory biomarkers, YXDJ was associated with reductions in hs-CRP [MD = -1.21 mg/L, P < 0.00001, low], TNF-α [SMD = -0.44, P = 0.0009, low], and IL-6 [MD = -10.42 ng/L, P < 0.00001, low]; subgroup analysis further showed a greater reduction in hs-CRP in postoperative patients [MD = -1.42 mg/L, P < 0.00001, low]. For safety, no clear increase in the overall incidence of adverse events was observed [RR = 0.58, P = 0.07, low]. Exploratory analyses from single studies suggested possible long-term benefits, including a lower reported risk of ischemic stroke and sustained reductions in AF recurrence and symptom scores at 9 months post-ablation; however, these findings are preliminary and require confirmation. CONCLUSION: Current evidence, derived exclusively from methodologically limited, small, single-center Chinese studies, provides only preliminary signals that YXDJ may offer possible additional benefits as an adjunct to conventional therapy for symptom control and postoperative management in AF. Most efficacy outcomes were supported by low- or very-low-certainty evidence, with only LVEF and postoperative AF recurrence at 6 months rated as moderate certainty. These findings should be regarded as exploratory and hypothesis-generating. YXDJ should not replace guideline-directed anticoagulation, rate or rhythm control, or catheter ablation. Rigorously designed trials are needed to confirm its efficacy and safety. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW: Identifier CRD420261286691.

articles.title: Short-course versus standard- or longer-course oral antibiotic therapy for pneumonia and lower respiratory tract infection in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Reducing unnecessary antibiotic exposure is a major priority in pediatric antimicrobial stewardship. The comparative effectiveness of short-course versus standard- or longer-course oral antibiotic therapy for uncomplicated bacterial infections in children remains uncertain. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether short-course oral antibiotic therapy increases clinical treatment failure compared with standard- or longer-course therapy in children with uncomplicated bacterial infections, with a primary focus on same-antibiotic pediatric pneumonia/lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) trials. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and CENTRAL were searched, supplemented by citation searching and trial registry review. Eligible studies enrolled children aged 0-18 years with uncomplicated bacterial infections treated with oral antibiotics in outpatient or ambulatory settings. The primary outcome was clinical treatment failure; broader pneumonia/LRTI and all-infection analyses were treated as sensitivity or exploratory analyses. Random-effects meta-analysis used risk ratios (RRs) and risk differences (RDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool. The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261339263). RESULTS: Fourteen randomized trials were included; nine same-antibiotic pneumonia/LRTI comparisons contributed to the primary pooled analysis. Short-course therapy was not associated with increased treatment failure (RR, 1.01; 95% CI, 0.92-1.11; I2 = 0.0%), and the absolute-effect analysis showed no meaningful difference (RD, 0.001; 95% CI, -0.010 to 0.013; I2 = 10.0%). A broad pneumonia/LRTI sensitivity analysis including different-antibiotic comparisons was also non-significant (RR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.66-1.33) but heterogeneous. The all-infection exploratory analysis was similarly non-significant (RR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.63-1.25) and interpreted cautiously given clinical heterogeneity. Of the 14 trials, 5 were at low risk of bias, 2 had some concerns, and 7 were at high risk. CONCLUSION: In same-antibiotic pediatric pneumonia/LRTI trials, short-course therapy was not associated with increased clinical treatment failure compared with standard- or longer-course therapy. Broader analyses across different antibiotic strategies and infection syndromes did not materially change this interpretation but showed substantial heterogeneity. These findings support cautious, infection-specific antibiotic duration reduction rather than broad generalization across all uncomplicated pediatric bacterial infections. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261339263, identifier CRD420261339263.

articles.title: Continuous infusion versus intermittent infusion of vancomycin: a systematic review and meta-analysis with a focus on nephrotoxicity, target attainment, and clinical outcomes.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Vancomycin is widely used for Gram-positive infections but has a narrow therapeutic window and significant nephrotoxicity risk. Whether continuous infusion (CI) offers advantages over intermittent infusion (II) remains debated. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to compare CI versus II vancomycin regarding nephrotoxicity, target attainment, clinical outcomes, and time to therapeutic target. METHODS: PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched from inception to March 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies comparing CI and II of vancomycin were included. Outcomes assessed were nephrotoxicity, target concentration attainment, clinical efficacy, microbiological clearance, mortality, and time to therapeutic target. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) or mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using random-effects models. RESULTS: A total of 23 studies comprising 3,053 patients were included. CI was associated with significantly reduced nephrotoxicity (OR = 0.62, 95% CI = 0.48-0.79, I2 = 42%), higher target attainment (OR = 2.85, 95% CI = 2.12-3.84, I2 = 38%), and shorter time to therapeutic target (MD = -1.52 days, 95% CI = -1.98 to -1.06, I2 = 67%). No significant differences were observed for clinical efficacy (OR = 1.12, 95% CI = 0.86-1.46), microbiological clearance (OR = 1.08, 95% CI = 0.72-1.62), or mortality (OR = 0.94, 95% CI = 0.71-1.25). CONCLUSION: Continuous infusion of vancomycin reduces nephrotoxicity risk, improves target attainment, and shortens time to therapeutic target compared with intermittent infusion, without compromising clinical efficacy or survival. These findings support CI as a preferred strategy in patients at heightened risk of renal injury. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261365683, identifier CRD420261365683.

articles.title: Benefit-risk profiling of advanced therapies in moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis: a clustered network meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: The therapeutic landscape for moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis (UC) has expanded with the introduction of oral small molecules and recently approved biologics. However, the scarcity of head-to-head trials necessitates indirect comparisons to clarify their relative positioning. We aimed to determine the comparative efficacy and tolerability hierarchy of approved and emerging advanced therapies, incorporating the most contemporary evidence. METHODS: We retrieved randomized controlled trials (RCTs) from major databases up to November 2025. Efficacy outcomes included clinical remission and endoscopic improvement; tolerability was evaluated via discontinuations due to adverse events. We employed Bayesian network meta-analysis and bivariate clustered ranking to visualize efficacy-tolerability profiles, stratifying by prior biologic exposure. RESULTS: A total of 32 RCTs were included. In the induction phase, Upadacitinib, Ustekinumab, and Risankizumab co-occupied the "most favorable" quadrant, combining high efficacy with superior tolerability. In the maintenance phase, Upadacitinib 30 mg demonstrated the highest-ranking probability for efficacy, while IL-23 antagonists (Guselkumab, Mirikizumab) and low-dose Upadacitinib exhibited a highly favorable efficacy-tolerability profile. Notably, in biologic-exposed patients, Upadacitinib demonstrated the highest relative efficacy among evaluated therapies, whereas Guselkumab emerged as a highly effective biologic alternative based on current estimates. CONCLUSION: Based on current network estimates, Upadacitinib is suggested among the most efficacious options for achieving clinical and endoscopic endpoints, particularly in refractory disease, while IL-23 antagonists present highly favorable tolerability profiles for maintenance without compromising efficacy. These findings support a tailored approach to drug selection, aligning patient-specific profiles of inflammatory burden with current evidence-based safety thresholds. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261292029, identifier CRD420261292029.

articles.title: Effective doses of propofol and oliceridine fumarate for painless hysteroscopy: a two-phase dose-finding study using Dixon's up-and-down method.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Painless hysteroscopy is widely performed in gynecological practice, yet achieving an optimal balance between anesthetic safety and patient comfort remains challenging. Combining propofol with oliceridine may mitigate respiratory depression and injection pain associated with conventional regimens, though the effective doses for this combination have not been established. This study sought to identify the optimal dose combination of propofol and oliceridine for use in painless hysteroscopy. METHODS: Fifty-one women scheduled for elective painless hysteroscopy were enrolled in this prospective, two-phase dose-finding study. In Phase I, all patients received a fixed 1 mg dose of oliceridine at induction; propofol was subsequently titrated from an initial 2 mg/kg using Dixon's up-and-down sequential method in 0.1 mg/kg intervals. Probit regression modeling was used to derive propofol ED50 and ED95, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) obtained via the delta method; isotonic regression served as sensitivity analysis. In Phase II, propofol was fixed at the Phase I ED50, and oliceridine was titrated from 1 mg in 0.1 mg increments, with ED50 and ED95 determined identically. An effective response was defined as no body movement, no frowning, and a Ramsay Sedation Score ≥5 during cervical dilation and hysteroscope insertion. Secondary outcomes included Nociception Level Index (NOX), Cerebral State Index (CSI), hemodynamic parameters, and adverse events. RESULTS: The ED50 and ED95 of propofol were 1.818 mg/kg (95% CI: 1.696-1.940) and 2.223 mg/kg (95% CI: 1.840-2.605), respectively. For oliceridine, the corresponding ED50 was 0.663 mg (95% CI: 0.605-0.720) and ED95 was 0.813 mg (95% CI: 0.692-0.934). Pearson goodness-of-fit tests confirmed adequate model fit for both phases (propofol: P = 0.755; oliceridine: P = 0.899), and isotonic regression yielded ED50 estimates within 3% of probit-derived values. Hemodynamic parameters remained stable throughout sedation, with no serious adverse events observed. CONCLUSION: The propofol-oliceridine appears to be a feasible option for painless hysteroscopy, with an acceptable safety profile provided that continuous airway monitoring is maintained. The ED50 and ED95 values observed in this study offer preliminary dosing guidance for outpatient practice. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=241260, identifier ChiCTR2500102118.

articles.title: Effects of different doses of esketamine as an adjunct to sufentanil-based patient-controlled intravenous analgesia on postoperative analgesia and opioid consumption following lumbar decompression surgery: a dose-finding randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of different doses of esketamine as an adjunct to sufentanil-based patient-controlled intravenous analgesia (PCIA) on postoperative analgesia and opioid consumption after lumbar decompression surgery and to explore its optimal risk-benefit dose. METHODS: A total of 120 patients scheduled for lumbar decompression surgery were randomly allocated to four groups. The control group (Group N, n = 30) received PCIA with sufentanil 2.5 μg/kg. To test the opioid-sparing hypothesis, the three experimental groups (Groups S1, S2, and S3, n = 30 each) received PCIA with a lower sufentanil dose (1.5 μg/kg) combined with esketamine at 0.25, 0.5, and 1.0 mg/kg, respectively. All PCIA solutions were diluted with normal saline to a total volume of 100 mL. The primary outcome was the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) pain score at rest. Secondary outcomes included sufentanil consumption, PCIA press counts, requirement for rescue analgesia, Ramsay Sedation Scale (RSS) scores, and oxidative-stress markers; safety endpoints were analyzed as exploratory outcomes. Postoperative adverse effects, including nausea, vomiting, dizziness, respiratory depression, hypotension, and psychiatric symptoms (dissociation or nightmares), were recorded and compared across the four groups. RESULTS: All esketamine-containing regimens (S1-S3) showed significantly lower VAS scores at all postoperative time points compared with Group N (P < 0.05), with no statistically significant difference among S1, S2, and S3. The 24-h sufentanil consumption, effective PCIA presses, and rescue analgesia demand were also significantly reduced (P < 0.05). However, Ramsay sedation scores increased dose-dependently (S3 > S2 > S1). At 4 h postoperatively, SOD activity was higher, and concentrations of MDA, GLU, and COR were lower in all esketamine-containing regimens compared with Group N. Although the overall incidence of adverse events was comparable, the high-dose group (S3) had a significantly increased incidence of hypotension and dissociative symptoms. CONCLUSION: Adding esketamine to a reduced-sufentanil PCIA regimen improved postoperative analgesia and reduced opioid consumption after lumbar decompression surgery. Analgesic benefit was similar across the tested doses (0.25-1.0 mg/kg), whereas dose-related adverse effects (sedation, hypotension, psychomimetic symptoms) increased with dose. These findings suggest that 0.25 mg/kg may provide a favorable efficacy-safety balance within the investigated dose range. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: http://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.aspx?proj=249890, Identifier: ChiCTR2500095890.

articles.title: Current status and prospects of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) in drug delivery for women's health.
articles.abstract: Women's health includes many biological and social challenges, such as reproductive disorders, maternal complications, osteoporosis, and gynecological cancers. Many current treatments have limitations like poor drug solubility, side effects, and lack of targeted delivery for female physiology. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), which are crystalline porous materials made of metal nodes and organic linkers, are being studied as advanced drug delivery systems to solve these problems. This review explains how MOF-based systems can be used in women's healthcare. MOFs like UiO-66 and ZIF-8 are used in targeted chemotherapy for breast and ovarian cancers. These systems are pH-responsive and ligand-functionalized, which improves treatment efficiency and reduces side effects. MOFs are also useful in bone health, where they help deliver calcium, vitamin D3, and other osteogenic ions for treating postmenopausal osteoporosis. MOFs are being explored for hormonal regulation, non-hormonal contraception, and treatment of gynecological infections. However, there are still challenges such as long-term safety, metal ion leakage, and the need for proper testing in maternal-fetal conditions. With further research on safe synthesis methods and toxicity evaluation, MOFs can become an important platform for personalized and effective treatments in women's health.

articles.title: Microorganism-integrated microneedles: emerging biohybrid platforms for next-generation therapeutics.
articles.abstract: The minimally invasive delivery of therapeutics across biological barriers is a major challenge in modern medicine. Microneedles (MNs) are novel platforms to address this challenge effectively. Simultaneously, the therapeutic potential of live microorganisms has been harnessed for various biomedical applications. The integration of living microorganisms with MNs has recently emerged as a promising strategy that combines minimally invasive delivery with dynamic biological functions. This review explores the integration of different microorganisms (probiotics, commensal bacteria, pathogenic and engineered bacteria, and microalgae) into MNs for various biomedical applications such as chronic skin conditions, wound dressing, cancer therapy, and intradermal vaccination. In preclinical studies, these platforms generally showed improved outcomes compared with free microorganisms, microorganism-free MNs, or conventional treatments used as controls. Furthermore, combining microorganisms with photothermal agents, sonosensitizers, antibiotics, and nanozymes can further enhance therapeutic performance. Synergistic mechanisms in these platforms - such as targeted pathogen killing, microenvironment remodeling (hypoxia alleviation and glucose consumption), and in situ generation of gases and metabolites - highlight their potential as a new class of localized therapies. Finally, the current challenges along with the future potential applications of these emerging platforms are discussed in detail.

articles.title: TMEM63B as a dual-function mechanosensitive channel and lipid scramblase: structural insights, physiological roles, and pharmacological potential.
articles.abstract: TMEM63B, a member of the transmembrane channel/scramblase (TCS) superfamily, functions as both a mechanosensitive and osmosensitive ion channel and a lipid scramblase. Recent structural and functional studies have begun to reveal the molecular basis underlying these dual functions. In this review, we summarize the current understanding of TMEM63B, focusing on its structural architecture, channel and scramblase conformations, activation mechanisms, physiological roles and therapeutic potential. Importantly, the broad tissue distribution and disease-associated mutations of TMEM63B-linked to developmental epileptic encephalopathy, hemolytic anemia, placental dysfunction, pulmonary insufficiency, and intestinal barrier defects-underscore its emerging pharmacological relevance. We discuss the therapeutic opportunities and challenges in targeting TMEM63B, including allosteric modulation of its mechanosensitive gating, isoform- and tissue-selective strategies to mitigate on-target off-tissue toxicity, and the potential of biologics such as the agonistic antibody YN9303-24 for loss-of-function disorders. These insights provide a framework for understanding the mechanistic diversity of TCS proteins, their physiological significance, and their translational potential as a new class of druggable mechanosensitive targets.

articles.title: Wnt/β-catenin signaling dysregulation in Alzheimer's disease and therapeutic opportunities.
articles.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by neuronal and neurovascular dysfunction. Wnt/β-catenin signaling is a highly conserved pathway that plays essential roles in central nervous system development and homeostasis, including regulation of neurogenesis, synaptic plasticity, neuronal survival, cerebrovascular development, and blood-brain barrier (BBB) maintenance. Growing evidence increasingly implicates disruption of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in multiple neuronal and neurovascular processes relevant to AD. This review summarizes current knowledge of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway and examines evidence linking its dysregulation to AD from human studies, omics datasets, experimental models, and patient-derived cellular systems. It focuses on endothelial Wnt/β-catenin dysfunction as a potential early contributor to BBB breakdown, rather than on neuronal Wnt signaling. We also emphasize its role in BBB development and maintenance, neurovascular dysfunction, and emerging evidence that endothelial Wnt/β-catenin impairment may contribute to BBB dysfunction in AD. Additionally, we discuss cell-type-specific effects of Wnt signaling and therapeutic strategies targeting glycogen synthase kinase (GSK-3β), extracellular Wnt antagonists, and BBB integrity. Although challenges remain regarding cell-type specificity, disease-stage dependence, safety, biomarker development, and the efficacy of preclinical-to-clinical translation for targeting the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, modulating Wnt/β-catenin signaling represents a potential therapeutic approach to preserve neuronal and neurovascular function in AD.

articles.title: Apolipoproteins in nanoparticle-mediated brain drug delivery: promise, mechanisms, and misconceptions.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Apolipoprotein E (apoE) plays a context-dependent role in nanomedicine for central nervous system drug delivery. It can facilitate cerebral endothelial recognition and increase brain exposure in nanoparticle systems while simultaneously promoting hepatic uptake, challenging its traditional interpretation as a brain-specific targeting ligand. AREAS COVERED: This review critically evaluates evidence from classical polysorbate-coated poly(butyl cyanoacrylate) (PBCA) and apoE-coupled albumin nanoparticles, apoE-derived peptide systems, solid lipid nanoparticles, and ionizable lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Attention is given to apoE presentation and isoform biology, protein-corona dynamics, LDL receptor family interactions, hepatic clearance, blood-brain barrier (BBB) status, route-dependent disposition, and blood-cell interactions. Advances in BBB models, LNP engineering, and translational strategies are also considered. EXPERT OPINION: ApoE should be regarded as a tunable regulator of nanoparticle biodistribution rather than a universal BBB shuttle. Development should focus on therapeutically active drug exposure in the relevant brain compartment rather than apoE binding, endothelial uptake, or total brain-associated signal. This requires assessment of whole-blood interactions, hepatic partitioning, receptor dependence, compartment-resolved brain disposition, payload release, pharmacodynamic activity, disease-specific BBB biology, and potentially apoE genotype. ApoE-based systems should be advanced only when they demonstrate a reproducible therapeutic advantage over comparable unmodified carriers and alternative brain-delivery strategies.

articles.title: An update on combinational chemo-immunotherapy for breast cancer using nanotechnology.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Breast cancer is still a considerable public health issue worldwide. However, earlier studies reported that chemotherapeutic drugs suppress the immune system. Therefore, a combination of chemotherapeutic agents with an immunomodulator might enhance antitumor immunity through immunogenic cell death, cross-priming, and the regulation of immune checkpoint molecules. AREA COVERED: Nanotechnology-enabled drug delivery has received considerable attention in chemo-immunotherapy. A comprehensive literature review was performed using google scholar, Science Direct, the Clinical Research Database, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and DOAJ. The review discusses the combination of immunotherapy and nanotechnology including AI-based techniques used to identify suitable biomarkers and to enable selective drug delivery to breast cancer cells. EXPERT OPINION: The combinational therapy containing chemotherapeutic agents and immunomodulators has shown promising results due to their synergistic effects. The application of artificial intelligence (AI) in nanomedicine has enabled the design of nanoparticles, predict their interactions with drugs, and personalize treatment based on patients' individual tumor profiles. This advancement has marked the advent of precision medicine in oncology, which focuses on tailoring therapies to each tumor's molecular and genetic profile. Despite these encouraging developments, several challenges remain in nanotechnology for cancer therapy, including mass production, biosafety, regulatory issues, and the successful translation of laboratory findings into clinical practice.

articles.title: Harnessing chemokines and nanocarriers to reprogram the tumor microenvironment.
articles.abstract: Although cancer immunotherapy has significantly altered the treatment landscape for malignant tumors, the intricate and diverse tumor microenvironment (TME) still limits its effectiveness in solid tumors. The TME is a complex and heterogeneous environment, shaped predominantly by chemokines rather than being a passive consequence of various biological processes. Therefore, it is essential to comprehend and fully utilize chemokine-guided immune cell navigation in order to overcome immunological rejection and increase the effectiveness of combination cancer therapy. In this review, we begin by summarizing the developing understanding of chemokine involvement in the TME. We then look at how distinct chemokine axes direct immune cells to different tumor areas, as well as the important elements that influence these processes. In addition, we discuss recent developments in integrating chemokines or chemokine receptors with nanodelivery technologies. These systems can stabilize chemokines, prolong local retention, create sustained gradients, and use chemokine-receptor interactions for targeted delivery. Overall, this review provides an updated framework for understanding chemokine-guided tumor immune modulation, as well as insights for developing next-generation nanomedicines and chemokine-based immunotherapeutic methods.

articles.title: Integrating multi-omics with machine learning: from genomic variant functional annotation to pharmacogenomics and biomarker discovery.
articles.abstract: Integrating heterogeneous multi-omics data with machine learning (ML) provides a powerful framework for interpreting genomic variants and advancing pharmacogenomic research in precision medicine. High-throughput technologies have generated vast datasets spanning genomics, transcriptomics, epigenomics, and proteomics, yet integrating these high-dimensional data into clinically meaningful insights remains a major computational challenge. Machine learning and deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), Transformers, and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), offer promising solutions. This narrative review provides a state-of-the-art overview of ML-driven multi-omics integration across early, intermediate, and late fusion paradigms. We highlight how these approaches may support functional variant interpretation, including the reclassification of Variants of Uncertain Significance (VUS), and emerging pharmacogenomic applications. Key areas include predictive biomarkers for drug efficacy, therapeutic resistance in precision oncology, and personalized dosing in rare and complex diseases. Finally, we discuss challenges related to data heterogeneity, clinical interpretability, and regulatory approval, as well as the requirements for translating emerging computational approaches into clinically validated pharmacogenomic practice and precision pharmacotherapy.

articles.title: Corticosteroids in septic shock: mechanisms, heterogeneous treatment effects, and trajectory-guided precision pharmacotherapy.
articles.abstract: Corticosteroid therapy in septic shock has evolved from empirical high-dose anti-inflammatory treatment to low-dose adjunctive pharmacotherapy aimed primarily at restoring vascular responsiveness and accelerating shock reversal. Population-level randomized evidence supports a modest average corticosteroid benefit, most consistently reflected in faster shock reversal and earlier vasopressor liberation, whereas mortality effects remain regimen- and population-dependent. This divergence suggests that average treatment effects alone are insufficient to guide individual decisions. We review how pharmacology, randomized evidence, candidate treatment-effect modifiers, and prespecified longitudinal phenotypes may inform the development of individualized corticosteroid strategies, while defining the evidence required before such strategies can guide clinical care. Glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid receptor biology provides plausible pathways for both benefit and harm, but no single mechanism, cortisol test, transcriptomic endotype, or clinical trajectory is currently validated for routine treatment selection. Candidate enrichment signals must be distinguished as prognostic, predictive, pharmacodynamic, or safety-related and must be available before corticosteroid exposure when used for treatment selection. Observational studies require explicit alignment of eligibility, time zero, treatment strategies, and follow-up; target trial emulation can reduce avoidable temporal bias but cannot substitute for randomization or remove unmeasured confounding. Trajectory-guided enrichment remains investigational: any candidate trajectory used for treatment selection must be assigned or predicted from information available before exposure, and differential treatment effects require explicit evaluation rather than prognostic association alone. Treatment evaluation should extend beyond mortality to shock reversal, organ-support liberation, kidney outcomes, metabolic toxicity, infection, neuromuscular effects, and longer-term function. Clinical decision support should remain a future, clinician-supervised implementation layer that translates validated evidence into time-stamped actions rather than an autonomous prescribing system. Progress toward precision corticosteroid therapy now requires prespecified enrichment hypotheses, direct regimen comparisons, harmonized outcomes, prospective validation, and trials demonstrating clinical utility.

articles.title: Research progress of polyunsaturated fatty acids in inflammatory bowel disease: from mechanisms to treatment.
articles.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) imposes a growing clinical burden through recurrent intestinal inflammation, malnutrition, treatment-related toxicity, and incomplete mucosal healing. Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are plausible dietary regulators of this burden, yet their effects cannot be reduced to a simple anti-inflammatory role for n-3 PUFAs and a pro-inflammatory role for n-6 PUFAs. The proposed pre-clinical concept of PUFA-induced metabolic enteritis links dietary lipid exposure to epithelial stress, lipid peroxidation, and intestinal inflammation in genetically or metabolically susceptible pre-clinical models. Its human counterpart, however, remains incompletely defined. This narrative review integrates evidence across PUFA-derived lipid mediators, the gut microbiota, intestinal barrier function, mucosal immunity, and the glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4)-ferroptosis axis. We distinguish observational associations from interventional evidence and examine why clinical trials of eicosapentaenoic acid and docosahexaenoic acid have produced inconsistent results. We also evaluate dietary patterns, PUFA supplements, microbiome-directed approaches, specialized pro-resolving mediators, oxylipin pathways, and soluble epoxide hydrolase inhibition. Current evidence remains pre-clinical. Our review provides an approach and insights for managing IBD before PUFA-directed interventions are incorporated into precision treatment for IBD.

articles.title: Advanced drug delivery and PBPK modelling as translational tools for precision therapies in juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
articles.abstract: Patients with persistent forms of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) often report limited therapeutic benefit from currently available treatments. Despite substantial advances in the management of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and related disorders over recent decades, treatment strategies for JIA remain insufficiently defined. The application of advanced drug delivery systems holds promise in addressing these limitations by enabling controlled and sustained drug release over extended periods. Other integrative approaches such as novel physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modelling have demonstrated to be a critical tool in optimizing pharmacotherapy in pediatric populations, particularly by improving dose selection and predicting drug disposition. This review summarizes current disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) for JIA management and critically examines the current, still largely prospective, integration of emerging drug delivery systems with PBPK modelling, highlighting existing translational examples alongside key opportunities and challenges for precision therapies in this field.

articles.title: Host determinants of immune-related adverse events during immune checkpoint inhibition.
articles.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the treatment of many cancers, but immune-related adverse events (irAEs) have become their principal limitation. This review argues that irAEs are not a random hazard of checkpoint blockade but a largely host-determined outcome layered on a drug-set baseline. The regimen fixes how much toxicity risk exists and, through the checkpoint it blocks, which organs are most likely affected. Within that envelope, host determinants decide which patient crosses the threshold of tolerance, and where. We synthesise the evidence for four classes of host determinant: germline genetic variation, including the IL7 locus and organ-directing human leucocyte antigen (HLA) alleles; the baseline immune landscape; the gut microbiome and metabolic state; and clinical characteristics led by pre-existing autoimmune disease. We draw two distinctions the literature often blurs. First, susceptibility should be read in two stages: determinants measurable before the first dose, which can triage patients, and on-treatment changes, which can only signal an event already emerging. Second, organ-specific toxicity is neither drug- nor host-intrinsic but the product of their intersection, with HLA restriction and shared tumour-tissue antigens offering the clearest mechanistic account of why a particular organ is struck. One theme runs throughout: many host features that raise irAE risk also predict a better antitumour response, so host stratification is a matter of optimising a benefit-to-toxicity balance rather than screening susceptible patients out. Multi-omics and systems immunology are assembling the measurements needed to act on this biology, but no host-based pre-treatment predictor is yet validated for clinical use. Realising one would shift checkpoint immunotherapy from the reactive management of toxicity toward its anticipation.

articles.title: Neutrophil dysregulation in sepsis-induced acute lung injury: mechanistic framework and therapeutic targeting by natural products.
articles.abstract: Sepsis-induced acute lung injury (SALI) is an important complication of sepsis associated with substantial morbidity and mortality, yet effective targeted therapies remain limited. Neutrophils are central effectors of innate immunity and play indispensable roles in early antimicrobial defense. However, during sepsis, persistent inflammatory stimulation drives neutrophil dysregulation, leading to excessive pulmonary infiltration, aberrant activation, delayed apoptosis, neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, and immune imbalance, all of which contribute to alveolar-capillary barrier disruption and lung injury progression. Emerging evidence indicates that neutrophil heterogeneity in SALI is shaped by multiple molecular regulators rather than by maturation status alone. Trafficking receptors, activation-associated markers, disease-associated transcriptional states, and intercellular signaling pathways-including CXCR4, CXCR2, CD11b, CD16, CD177, Fth1, Prok2, CD64/CD271, PD-L1, and Notch1-related signaling-collectively regulate neutrophil trafficking, activation, effector responses, and crosstalk with endothelial and immune cells. In this review, we summarize the molecular determinants underlying neutrophil functional heterogeneity and discuss the dual role of neutrophils in host defense and tissue injury in SALI. We also highlight the major mechanisms of neutrophil-mediated lung damage and summarize emerging evidence that natural products can alleviate SALI by modulating neutrophil recruitment, oxidative stress, inflammatory signaling, and NET formation. Targeting neutrophil dysregulation represents a potential therapeutic approach that requires further mechanistic and clinical validation.

articles.title: Carbon dots derived from traditional Chinese medicines: a novel therapeutic strategy for ocular diseases.
articles.abstract: Carbon dots (CDs) represent a novel category of zero-dimensional carbon-based nanomaterials featuring favorable biosafety in vitro and in acute animal studies. They also exhibit distinctive optical properties and diverse pharmacological activities. Synthesized via eco-friendly green routes using traditional Chinese medicines (TCMs) and their extracts, TCM-derived carbon dots (TCM-CDs) display distinct properties compared to conventional nanocarriers. Benefiting from their inherent nanostructures, abundant surface functional groups, and nanozyme-like activity, TCM-CDs can deliver intrinsic therapeutic effects without loading exogenous drugs or relying on residual herbal ingredients. They possess multiple bioactivities, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antibacterial and neuroprotective effects, which make them potential non-invasive therapeutic candidates for refractory ocular disorders. A growing body of studies has validated the promising therapeutic efficacy of TCM-CDs in animal models against autoimmune uveitis, retinal lesions, and optic nerve injuries, highlighting their encouraging preclinical findings that warrant further investigation toward clinical translation. Focusing on the intrinsic therapeutic capacity of TCM-CDs, this review systematically summarizes their core functional mechanisms and research progress in ocular disease intervention, discusses prevailing academic controversies and unresolved research bottlenecks in this field, and proposes prospective developmental directions. This work intends to offer comprehensive theoretical evidence and guidance directions for subsequent mechanistic investigations and clinical translation of TCM-CDs in ophthalmic research.

articles.title: Traumatic brain injury, neurobiology of aggression and antisocial behavior: from large-scale brain networks to anatomical and molecular substrates.
articles.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) triggers a dynamic pathological cascade that often culminates in chronic neuropsychiatric sequelae, such as reactive aggression and antisocial behavior. While these debilitating manifestations severely impair social reintegration and quality of life, their heterogeneous nature complicates clinical and forensic characterization. This review addresses this challenge through an integrated, multiscale framework that bridges macro-scale network desynchronization with micro-circuit pathology. We illustrate how the mechanical disruption of major white matter tracts decouples large-scale neurocognitive networks, leaving subcortical emotional anchors in a state of unmodulated hyper-reactivity stripped of prefrontal inhibitory control. The macroscopic untethering operates in synergy with localized cellular failures within specific amygdalar subnuclei, where chronic neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and ascending neuromodulatory alterations durably shift the affective circuitry toward a hyperexcitable state. By mapping these dimensional neurobiological substrates directly onto the DSM-5-TR taxonomic framework, we spark a new neuroforensic debate regarding criminal responsibility, considering the boundaries of volitional control and the contemporary debate on free will in organically compromised patients. This translational perspective guides the evaluation of novel therapeutic strategies, shifting the paradigm away from non-specific pharmacological sedation toward personalized, state-dependent neuromodulation capable of exogenously restoring circuit synchrony and patient clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Natural polysaccharides as modulators of mitochondrial homeostasis: structural determinants, pharmacological mechanisms, and translational challenges.
articles.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is a convergent pathological feature of neurodegenerative, metabolic, cardiovascular, hepatic, and cancer-related disorders, making mitochondrial homeostasis an important therapeutic target. Natural polysaccharides (NPs) are structurally diverse macromolecules that have emerged as promising multifunctional modulators of mitochondrial homeostasis. This review summarizes the structural basis and mechanistic actions underlying the mitochondrial regulatory effects of NPs. Key structural features, including molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, glycosidic linkages, branching patterns, and chemical modifications, largely determine the mitochondria-regulating potential of NPs. Mechanistically, NPs regulate mitochondrial homeostasis by restoring bioenergetic function, reducing oxidative stress, maintaining mitochondrial quality control, and modulating mitochondria-dependent apoptosis. These effects support disease-context-specific therapeutic benefits, as NPs generally preserve mitochondrial homeostasis in non-malignant diseases while potentially inducing mitochondrial stress and cell death in cancer. This review also highlights key translational barriers to NP-based mitochondrial therapy, underscoring the need for standardized structural characterization, mechanism-oriented mitochondrial assays, and disease-specific evaluation.

articles.title: Research progress on the application of multi-scale computational methods in the research and development of anti-tuberculosis infection drugs.
articles.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), driven by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), remains a leading cause of mortality from infectious disease worldwide.​ The global dissemination of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) strains-coupled with protracted treatment regimens and the persistence of latent infection-has not only compromised first-line chemotherapies but also underscored the stagnation of conventional drug development pipelines. In this review, we systematically synthesize how multi-scale computational strategies are reshaping anti-TB drug discovery and explicitly delineate their hierarchical integration-a cohesive framework that, to our knowledge, has yet to be comprehensively mapped in the existing literature.​ We survey four interconnected computational layers: (i) systems and network pharmacology for macroscopic target and pathway prioritization; (ii) machine learning (ML) for mesoscopic virtual screening, resistance classification, and ADMET prediction; (iii) molecular docking for microscopic elucidation of ligand-target binding modes; and (iv) molecular dynamics (MD) simulations for atomic-level validation of binding poses and assessment of complex stability. Representative studies demonstrate that this workflow has pinpointed pivotal TB vulnerabilities (e.g., MmpL3, InhA, DprE1, ATP synthase, and FtsZ), enabled ML models to predict drug resistance from genomic data with high fidelity, and identified promising candidates such as vazabitide A (predicted binding affinity of -85.8 kcal/mol against Pks13) alongside repurposed agents (e.g., aldoxorubicin, quarfloxin). Critically, these computational predictions are reinforced by orthogonal experimental validation spanning in vitro enzymatic and phenotypic assays, in vivo infection models, clinical pharmacokinetic profiling, and multi-omics corroboration. We conclude that the top-down pipeline-spanning network pharmacology to ML, docking, and MD-integrated with bottom-up feedback constitutes a closed-loop paradigm that accelerates lead identification while addressing emergent drug resistance.​ Nevertheless, inherent limitations in predictive reliability and cross-layer error propagation necessitate rigorous downstream experimental validation. Looking forward, generative artificial intelligence, self-driving laboratories, and standardized cross-method benchmarking are poised to consolidate this multi-scale pipeline into a robust engine for next-generation anti-TB therapeutics.

articles.title: Targeting pain where it CouNts: the role of neurotensin signaling in pain and analgesia.
articles.abstract: Chronic pain affects more than one-fifth of adults in the United States and represents a major public health burden due to its impact on quality of life, productivity, and healthcare costs. Current pharmacological treatments remain limited in efficacy and are often associated with significant adverse effects, highlighting the need for safer and more effective therapeutic strategies. Neurotensin (Nts), a neuropeptide widely expressed in the central and peripheral nervous systems, has emerged as an important modulator of nociceptive processing. Nts signals through the G protein-coupled receptors neurotensin receptor 1 (NTSR1) and neurotensin receptor 2 (NTSR2), which are expressed in key neuroanatomical components of pain pathways. In this review, we summarize current knowledge of the neuronal and molecular mechanisms underlying pain processing and discuss how Nts signaling modulates nociceptive transmission at peripheral, spinal, and supraspinal levels. In addition to regulating nociceptor excitability and spinal excitatory neurotransmission, Nts critically regulates neural circuits involved in descending pain modulation, including the periaqueductal gray and rostral ventromedial medulla, and contributes to pain processing within limbic and hypothalamic networks that integrate sensory and affective components of pain. Finally, we discuss recent advances in pharmacological modulation of Nts receptors, including biased allosteric modulators and receptor-selective agonists that show promising analgesic efficacy in preclinical models. Together, these findings position the neurotensin system as a promising target for the development of novel non-opioid therapies for pain.

articles.title: Interpreting antiretroviral exposure and drug-drug interactions in pregnancy: A clinically anchored framework for HIV pharmacology.
articles.abstract: In pregnancy, antiretroviral drug-drug interactions must be interpreted against dynamic changes in gastrointestinal physiology, plasma-protein binding, renal elimination, hepatic enzyme activity and membrane transporter expression. Interaction studies quantify geometric mean exposure ratios relative to nonpregnant adults, but these measures describe relative pharmacokinetic change rather than whether effective exposure is preserved. For HIV treatment, validated exposure-response targets remain reasonable starting anchors when pregnancy-specific targets are unavailable. No evidence indicates that gestational immune adaptation alone requires a different intrinsic antiviral target. Pregnancy alters target attainment by altering drug disposition and variability, and it can modify the pharmacokinetics of both the victim antiretroviral and the perpetrator drug. For long-acting injectable PrEP, protective exposure, dosing interval and pharmacokinetic tail require separate consideration from treatment targets. This review evaluates candidate evidentiary anchors, including protein-adjusted in vitro inhibitory concentrations, exposure-response relationships, therapeutic drug-monitoring targets and model-informed probability of target attainment. Evidence from integrase inhibitors, protease inhibitors, non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, tenofovir formulations and long-acting agents demonstrates that similar proportional reductions in exposure can have different clinical implications depending on therapeutic margin, resistance barrier, interaction mechanism, formulation and pharmacologically relevant matrix. A newly proposed six-domain framework integrates clinical context, active analyte, exposure metric, evidentiary anchor, distributional target attainment and clinical outcomes. Physiologically based and population pharmacokinetic models provide evidence when pregnancy-specific data are unavailable, but their use should reflect model verification and uncertainty. The central objective is therefore not to define a universal pregnancy threshold but to determine whether pharmacologically effective exposure is maintained in the setting of gestational physiology and concomitant medicines.

articles.title: Engineered probiotic-mediated palmitoylethanolamide biosynthesis protects against colitis-associated liver injury.
articles.abstract: Chronic colitis promotes secondary liver injury through disruption of the gut-liver axis, whereby intestinal barrier breakdown enables portal translocation of microbial products that activate hepatic inflammatory and fibrogenic pathways. Palmitoylethanolamide (PEA), an endogenous ALIAmide acting primarily via PPAR-α, exerts anti-inflammatory and barrier-protective effects, but its clinical use is limited by poor oral bioavailability. We investigated whether mucosa-targeted, probiotic-mediated, in situ PEA biosynthesis could attenuate liver injury associated with chronic colitis. Male C57BL/6J mice were subjected to chronic dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) colitis and treated with an engineered Lactobacillus paracasei F19 strain expressing human NAPE-PLD (pNAPE-LP) plus ultra-low-dose palmitate, a control strain (pLP), or pNAPE-LP combined with the PPAR-α antagonist MK886. pNAPE-LP significantly increased colonic PEA levels and elevated circulating and hepatic PEA, confirming effective local production with systemic distribution. Treatment ameliorated colitis severity, restored tight-junction protein expression, and reduced endotoxemia. Importantly, pNAPE-LP attenuated colitis-associated liver injury by decreasing histological damage and collagen deposition, lowering transaminase levels, and reducing hepatic neutrophil infiltration. These effects were accompanied by the suppression of the hepatic TLR4/NF-κB/NLRP3 inflammasome axis, reduced caspase-1 activation, decreased IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6 levels, restored PPAR-α expression, and reduced Bax expression.
